items.title: AI Literacy and Ethical Voice in Algorithmic Hiring: The Mediating Role of Psychological Safety and Moral Efficacy
items.abstract: Responsible human resource management (HRM) relies on human oversight, which works only when people are willing to question problematic algorithmic outputs. Based on social cognitive theory and psychological safety theory, this study investigates whether there is a direct link between AI literacy and the ethical voice in algorithms for hiring, as well as whether there is an indirect link through psychological safety and moral efficacy. Data of the survey in the form of information was collected from 390 employees who were engaged in recruitment and selection process in four multinational companies in Pakistan (purposive sampling; 470 questionnaires were distributed). The regression and bootstrap analyses revealed that the variables of psychological safety (B = 0.31) and moral efficacy (B = 0.37) had a positive relationship with AI literacy, while the direct path from ethical voice to AI literacy showed a stronger effect (total effect B = 0.44, p < .001). Psychological safety and moral efficacy both predicted ethical voice, and there was an indirect relationship between psychological safety and moral efficacy. Indirect effects made up approximately 42% of the overall effect, and there were significant indirect paths via psychological safety, via moral efficacy, and sequentially via both psychological safety and moral efficacy, in addition to a significant direct path (complementary partial mediation). AI-literacy training in combination with a safe reporting climate and high moral efficacy might therefore be most likely to help supervise ethical use. Data are cross-sectional in nature and self-reported, so the results are interpreted in terms of associations.

items.abstract: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.

items.title: AI-Assisted Regulatory Intelligence and Adaptive Compliance Verification System for Banking Supervision
items.abstract: Regulatory requirements issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) fall into categories including numerical thresholds, deterministic conditions, temporal obligations, and qualitative standards such as ''adequate due diligence,'' each of which requires a different mode of verification. Bank employees and officers must first locate and interpret the appropriate requirement among an ever-growing corpus of Master Directions, circulars, and notifications, while the regulator must independently verify (at scale) whether submitted bank evidence satisfies the requirement. We present a two-module regulatory intelligence system that addresses both sides of this problem in a single pipeline. The Regulation Comprehension module ingests an RBI circular or Master Direction and segments and categorizes its clauses, extracts a typed and machine-readable rule representation, simplifies regulatory language for reading by humans, and enables natural-language question answering with clause-level sourcing. The main technical contribution is an adaptive reasoning-modality router that determines, for a given regulatory requirement and evidence set, whether a deterministic rule engine, a retrieval-based large language model (LLM), or human escalation should be used, governed by an explicit cost--accuracy--latency objective and a hard architectural override that directs fully specified deterministic rules and complete evidence to the rule engine unconditionally. This differs from the well-studied task of routing between LLMs of differing capability, since our router chooses among fundamentally different reasoning mechanisms rather than among models. We also contribute a rule-grounded synthetic RBI compliance benchmark across nine difficulty categories and a dedicated regulation-comprehension benchmark design (with extraction, question-answering, and simplification variants), such that the two modules can be evaluated with equal rigor rather than treating comprehension as a subordinate preprocessing step, yielding two distinct sets of metrics, baselines, and ablation points, each for one of the modules, across extraction accuracy, retrieval and answer-faithfulness, simplification quality, compliance accuracy, and routing efficiency. We also contribute an evidence-grounded explanation architecture that traces every such decision and comprehension answer to a specific rule, clause, and evidentiary or source field. Since operational bank data cannot be accessed for confidentiality and regulatory reasons, evaluation is performed on a synthetic, rule-grounded benchmark of 1,393 cases drawn from 215 rules. On the 294 held-out test cases, whose rules were never seen in training or tuning, the adaptive router reaches 92.2\% automated accuracy and 96.9\% end-to-end accuracy, compared with 85.4\% for a fixed hybrid router, 72.5\% for retrieval-augmented LLM-only reasoning, and 56.8\% for LLM-only reasoning, and ablations show that removing adaptive routing, the rule engine, or evidence grounding lowers accuracy. Adversarial and ambiguous cases remain the hardest. All results are on synthetic rather than operational bank data, the decisions of the LLM reasoning paths in these runs were produced by a deterministic surrogate of the LLM judge, and results of the regulation-comprehension benchmark are not reported in this paper.

items.title: AI-Assisted Visual Search: Effects of Cueing Method and Display Type on Detection, Compliance, and Skill Retention
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection systems can enhance visual search in safety-critical domains, yet how they present recommendations may determine their effectiveness under display-quality constraints. We compared three cueing methods: an indirect cue signaling only presence (textual alert) and two direct cues marking the target’s location through either signal enhancement (bounding box) or noise reduction (contextual blur), across color and monochrome displays. Participants (N = 122) searched maritime aerial imagery in a fixed-order block structure (unaided, aided, unaided). Direct cues improved detection only under monochrome conditions, whereas the indirect cue lowered joint human–AI accuracy below that of the AI alone. Bounding boxes yielded the highest detection, whereas contextual blur reduced response times and increased compliance. Temporal analyses revealed that aided performance diverged from retained skill, with blur the most durable after withdrawal despite stronger signs of automation dependence. Cueing should be matched to display type and operational context, and judged by the skill that persists after support.

items.title: AI-Enabled Pedagogy: Enhancing Teaching Practice and Student Learning With Genai in Distance Education
items.abstract: This article explores the innovative potential of generative artificial intelligence in distance education and focuses on its application to enhance teaching practice and student learning. The concept of AI-enabled pedagogy is introduced, where lecturers utilise generative artificial intelligence tools to create personalised, adaptive, and immersive learning experiences. A case study of a distance education module illustrates the effective integration of generative artificial intelligence in teaching practices and highlights its benefits in the automation of repetitive tasks, provision of synchronous feedback, and the facilitation of collaborative learning. The article also examines the challenges and limitations of implementing generative artificial intelligence in distance education which include concerns related to academic integrity, bias, and digital literacy. The findings of this study include perspectives into the potential of generative artificial intelligence to transform teaching and learning in distance education. The article provides implications for lecturers, policymakers, and researchers, and highlights future directions for research on GAI in distance education.

items.title: AI, Employee Productivity and Performance: An Integrated ISM–MICMAC and SEM Investigation of the Pathway from Organisational Investment to Individual Output
items.abstract: Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and discriminant validity thresholds. Human-AI task complementarity is the strongest proximal predictor of productivity and performance, followed at some distance by trust in AI and by job insecurity, which carries a negative sign. AI governance and reskilling investment have indirect effects, albeit small but reliable, that are passed on through the process of trust. However, job insecurity undermines the complementarity-performance relationship, although the interaction does not contribute much (under one percent) to the explained variance and should be avoided. The two phases imply that investment in artificial intelligence to boost productivity primarily is reshaping jobs and the context in which they exist.

items.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

items.title: An AI-Driven Multimodal Data Integration Framework for Holistic Patient Profiling in Healthcare Robotics
items.abstract: With the fast development of healthcare data, there is a lot of opportunities are there for artificial intelligence (AI) to make improvement in disease diagnosis, patient monitoring, and clinical decision-making. While heterogeneous distribution of healthcare information makes comprehensive patient analysis challenging. This paper proposes a multimodal framework AIMDI-HR (AI-Driven Multimodal Data Integration for Holistic Patient Profiling in Healthcare Robotics), that integrates Electronic Health Records (EHR) and physiological vital-sign data which supports intelligent patient profiling and hearth disease prediction. This proposed framework concludes data pre-processing, feature normalization, multimodal data integration, prediction based on machine-learning, and feature importance analysis. In this paper three supervised machine learning models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were estimated using a multimodal dataset which is built from healthcare datasets which are publicly available. After the experiment, the results signify that the Random Forest model got the highest performance with 90.16% accuracy, 89.29% F1-score, and 0.9448 ROC-AUC. Also feature importance analysis indicates contribution of both clinical and physiological features toward predication of disease. The proposed framework shows ability of multimodal AI techniques to increase predictive healthcare system and gives support for decisions for future healthcare robotic applications.

items.title: An assistive Braille proofreading system for empowering lay volunteers
items.abstract: Braille literature serves as a critical conduit for individuals with visual impairments to access information, deepen learning, and achieve professional self-actualization (Ryles, 1996). However, transcribing Chinese texts into Taiwanese Braille poses unique and formidable challenges. Unlike alphabetic languages, Chinese is a logographic language consisting of thousands of distinct characters. Crucially, Taiwanese Braille does not directly map onto Chinese characters but is instead intrinsically bound to their phonetic values via the Zhuyin system (Hung, 2008). Consequently, a single character can carry entirely different pronunciations and Braille representations depending on its semantic context, rendering polyphonic characters the primary bottleneck in automated transcription. Beyond Taiwanese Braille, Japanese Braille confronts analogous hurdles in homonym confusion (Seto et al., 2023)—the inverse of the polyphonic challenge—reflecting a persistent dilemma across character-based Asian orthographies. To correct errors induced by polyphonic ambiguities, Braille literature must undergo rigorous proofreading prior to publication. Traditional proofreading relies heavily on cumbersome manual workflows, typically executed via two approaches: a collaborative dyad of a visually impaired reader and a sighted volunteer, or an individual expert proficient in both Chinese characters and Braille. This acute dependency on specialized human resources severely delays Braille literature production, stifling the timely supply of accessible learning materials and thereby impeding digital equity. To alleviate this persistent societal dilemma and promote inclusive learning design, this study developed a web-based assistive platform, Braille Reviser (B-Reviser). Bridging human empathy and algorithmic efficiency, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to independently correct Braille errors simply by modifying familiar Zhuyin (phonetic) symbols. Developed on a LAMP architecture, B-Reviser integrates the CNS11643 Full Character Library from Taiwan’s Government Open Data Platform to construct a robust character-to-phonetic baseline. To resolve the most intractable contextual ambiguities of polyphonic characters, B-Reviser leverages the Gemini Large Language Model for deep semantic analysis, substantially reducing transcription errors prior to human verification. Within the user interface, each Chinese character is rendered alongside its corresponding Zhuyin and Braille representations, with polyphonic characters visually highlighted to guide user attention. For any displayed character, clicking its Zhuyin displays all alternative pronunciations (as illustrated in Figure 1 below), while clicking the character itself links directly to an online Chinese dictionary for real-time reference. This workflow effectively dismantles the expertise barrier inherent in traditional proofreading, enabling lay volunteers to achieve precise correction autonomously. Ultimately, this human-centered proofreading platform addresses long-standing goals in assistive technology (Bhowmick & Hazarika, 2017). Preliminary evaluations demonstrate that B-Reviser significantly reduces technical thresholds, operational complexity, and task duration for volunteers. Centered on digital inclusion, this system exemplifies human-centric crowdsourcing design as a form of compassionate technology. Through human-artificial intelligence collaboration, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to accelerate the production of Braille literature, thereby promoting accessible learning and digital inclusion for individuals with visual impairments (Hersh & Johnson, 2008).

items.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
items.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

items.title: Analisis Kebutuhan Video Dokumenter Peristiwa Padang Area dalam Pembelajaran Sejarah
items.abstract: This study analyzes the need for a documentary video on the Padang Area Incident as a history-learning medium at SMKN 4 Padang. The study was positioned as the analysis stage of an ADDIE-oriented development study and employed a descriptive mixed-method design. Participants comprised one history teacher and 30 Grade XI Marketing students selected purposively. Data were collected through classroom observation, a teacher interview, and a student needs questionnaire. Quantitative data were summarized using frequencies and percentages, while qualitative data were condensed, categorized, displayed, and interpreted through technique triangulation. The findings show that history learning still relies mainly on lectures and textbooks, whereas digital media are not yet used consistently. Classroom observation indicated that only 43% of students displayed attention, 40% curiosity, 33% active involvement, and 27% intrinsic motivation. Students and the teacher therefore need a concise, contextual, and smartphone-accessible documentary that combines chronology, maps, archival visuals, narration, source attribution, and inquiry prompts. The Padang Area Incident is relevant to Phase F learning outcomes concerning Indonesia’s struggle to defend independence and supports the contextualization of national history through local history. These findings provide an empirical basis for developing the documentary; however, its validity, practicality, and effectiveness require further testing.

items.title: Analyse, create, defend: Securing human judgement in marketing communications assessment under generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI has unsettled a long-standing assumption in higher education: that a written submission is evidence of the thinking behind it. This is a particular problem in marketing communications education, where the capabilities that matter most, reading persuasion critically and arguing for a stronger alternative, are those a language model can now imitate. This paper offers a reflective account of an assessment designed in response, currently running in a postgraduate marketing communications subject at an Australian university. Students work in self-selected groups to analyse a real advertisement, then propose and present an improved version as a Pecha Kucha, before defending their decisions in a live discussion with the class and tutor. Generative AI is permitted for producing slide visuals but not for the analysis or argument. The paper argues that a rule of this kind cannot secure an assessment on its own, since compliance cannot be verified, and that what secures the task is the oral defence: a student who has not done the thinking cannot reconstruct it under questioning. This reframing draws on recent work distinguishing discursive from structural assessment change.

items.title: Analysis of counterflow-induced congestion propagation in a high-rise office building staircase: evidence from a full-building phased evacuation drill
items.abstract: In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

items.title: Analysis of Teacher Creativity in Media Development for Pancasila Education in the Digital Era at State Senior High School 9 Ambon
items.abstract: The transformation of 21st-century learning necessitates the integration of digital media to enhance students' cognitive engagement; however, its utilization in Pancasila Education at regional schools remains predominantly conventional due to disparities in infrastructure and technological literacy. The novelty of this study lies in the empirical mapping of teacher creativity dimensions in contextually designing audio, visual, and audio-visual media within an archipelagic region characterized by infrastructural constraints a context rarely examined in civic education literature. This study aims to analyze the level of teacher creativity in developing these three types of digital instructional media in Pancasila Education at SMA Negeri 9 Ambon. Employing a descriptive quantitative approach with a survey method, data were collected from the entire population of 44 eleventh-grade students (total sampling) using a closed-ended four-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics. The findings reveal that student agreement regarding teacher creativity reached 90% for audio media development ( ; ), 84% for visual media ( ; ), and 80% for audio-visual media ( ; ). These results indicate that teachers are more adaptive in developing standalone audio and visual media, whereas the utilization of audio-visual media is impeded by limited projectors, unstable internet connectivity, and preparation time constraints. Theoretically, this study enriches the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) discourse in resource-constrained settings, while practically recommending continuous training in interactive media production and the equitable distribution of school ICT infrastructure.

items.title: AnyAct: Towards Human Reenactment of Character Motion From Video
items.abstract: We study the problem of directly deriving an initial human reenactment from a monocular video of a non-human character. Our goal is not to reconstruct the source character itself but to reinterpret its motion as a plausible and editable human performance for downstream animation authoring. This task is challenging because existing video-based motion capture methods are largely restricted to human-centric structural spaces, while motion retargeting methods typically require structured 3D source motions and known source topologies. Our key insight is that sparse local articulated motion cues can preserve essential dynamics across large structural differences, providing a stable bridge from character video to human reenactment. Based on this observation, we propose AnyAct, which formulates character-video-driven human reenactment as conditional human motion generation from transferable sparse local 2D articulated motion. To make this practical, we introduce three key designs: human-motion-only supervision via augmented 3D-to-2D projection, progressive 3D-to-2D training to alleviate conditioning ambiguity, and global-local motion decoupling for reliable local motion control. We further construct a benchmark primarily covering diverse non-human character videos. Experiments on the benchmark show that AnyAct produces high-fidelity initial human reenactments that preserve the essential dynamics of the characters in reference videos, and further ablation studies validate the effectiveness of its core designs. Results are best visualized through https://anyact.github.io.

items.title: Are All Instances Equally Explainable? A Study on the Impact of Locality on the Explainability of Automatic Text Classification Tasks
items.abstract: Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.

items.title: Artefact or evidence? Clarifying what counts in programmatic learning portfolios
items.abstract: Australian higher education is moving toward programmatic assessment, a shift given further impetus by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency’s (TEQSA) 2023 discussion paper on assessment reform in the age of artificial intelligence. This calls for a systemic approach to program assessment aligned with disciplines and qualifications, rather than one confined to individual units (Lodge et al., 2023). Within this shift, the digital portfolio has become a mechanism for evidencing achievement across whole degree programs. Portfolios in this context typically hold a growing accumulation of materials such as assignments, placement records, project outputs, and reflective writing. As students collect artefacts across a program, the portfolio becomes a means of making their learning visible over time, reframing assessment as an ongoing process of meaning making rather than a series of isolated judgements (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). This poster argues that the value of a portfolio depends less on the volume of material it holds than on a distinction that is often assumed rather than made explicit: the difference between an artefact and evidence. An artefact is any product or record of student activity: an assignment, presentation, a reflection. It becomes evidence only once interpreted against a stated outcome or standard, connecting the artefact to the claim is meant to support (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). Without this connection, a portfolio functions as a repository of activity rather than a demonstration of learning. This distinction carries weight in programmatic assessment, where judgement is distributed rather than concentrated in a single task, and students and academic staff track development across a program of study. A set of specified standards is defined for each level of the program, which students must attain by the end of each phase. High-stakes decisions at these milestones are made by a panel weighing multiple, longitudinal artefacts against a program’s stated outcomes. This shift improves the defensibility and transparency of judgement while making learning visible over time (Baartman et al., 2022). Treated simply as collection points, portfolios risk becoming unwieldy and meaningless. When the artefact-evidence distinction is built into portfolio design, teaching and staff development from the outset, it offers a mechanism for students and programs to make cumulative, defensible claims about learning and graduate capabilities. This poster presents a framework distinguishing artefact from evidence, developed through curriculum transformation work at an Australian university moving toward programmatic learning. It sets out three conditions under which an artefact functions as evidence: alignment to a named outcome or standard, an explicit reflective or interpretive act connecting the artefact to that outcome, and a level of specificity that allows a marker or reviewer to assess the claim rather than merely acknowledge the artefact’s existence. The framework is intended as a practical reference point for curriculum designers, staff, and students working with portfolios in programmatic contexts. Delegates are invited to discuss how this distinction might apply, in their own programmatic curriculum work, where it breaks down in practice, and what it asks of the human relationship between student and assessor.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in diabetes mellitus: a tertiary review of the current landscape and future research directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming diabetes mellitus (DM) care by enabling earlier detection, precision management, and data-driven decision support across clinical settings. However, the growing number of systematic reviews has produced a fragmented evidence base, making it difficult to assess the field’s maturity, methodological quality, and clinical readiness, and leaving future research directions largely undefined. To clarify this landscape, we conducted a tertiary review that synthesizes 70 systematic reviews on AI applications across type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes and their major complications. Our analysis reveals an accelerating research trajectory since 2020, yet activity remains concentrated in type 1 and type 2 diabetes and in image-based applications such as diabetic retinopathy and foot-ulcer screening, with gestational and kidney disease still underexplored. Methodological rigor is inconsistent, with wide variation in search coverage, quality appraisal, and reporting standards. Across the literature, recurrent challenges include data bias, limited external validation, and barriers to clinical implementation. By integrating evidence across disease types, data modalities, and levels of care, this review shows that AI in diabetes is at a transitional stage. The field is technically advanced yet remains clinically fragmented and lacks a coherent roadmap for translation into practice. Expanding research into underrepresented areas such as multimodal data integration, natural-language processing of clinical text, and reinforcement learning for adaptive decision support will be essential to bridge this gap. This synthesis consolidates over a decade of secondary evidence and clarifies the structural and methodological requirements for achieving trustworthy, equitable, and scalable AI-driven diabetes care.

items.title: Artisanal and Historical Gold Mining: A Comparative Study Between Mozambique and Italy Toward Sustainable and Circular Practices
items.abstract: Gold mining takes place within highly diverse geological, technological, and socio-economic contexts, ranging from active artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) to historical gold mining districts where extraction has ceased, leaving long-term environmental legacies. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two case studies, active ASM in Mozambique and historical gold mining in Italy, examining how different stages of the mining life cycle shape environmental and social outcomes. In Mozambique, ASM remains a key rural livelihood but is associated with mercury amalgamation, siltation, and occupational health risks under largely informal conditions, with formalization constrained by artisanal extraction methods and access to finance, although cooperative organizational models and technical support services can help to overcome these constraints. In Italy, decades after mine closure, extractive waste and tailings continue to release potentially toxic elements while showing enrichment in critical raw materials (CRMs), representing anthropogenic resource stocks with secondary raw material recovery potential. Despite their different stages of activity, both case studies reveal opportunities for improving resource efficiency through circular economy approaches, mercury-free processing, geoconservation and geotourism, and integration of cultural heritage into territorial development. The comparison highlights the value of governance, capacity building, and knowledge transfer between active and post-mining contexts, supporting a shift toward more sustainable and circular gold mining practices.

items.title: Assessing the Effects of Design Complexity and Prompt Engineering on CAD Model Generation Using Microsoft Copilot
items.abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing across various sectors, making tasks more accessible, efficient, and user-friendly. One emerging application is computer-aided design (CAD), where AI has the potential to enable users with little or no-prior CAD experience to create three-dimensional (3D) models through natural-language. Despite growing interest in AI-assisted design, the capability of publicly accessible generative AI systems to reliably generate CAD models across varying levels of design complexity remains insufficiently studied. This work benchmarks the performance of Microsoft Copilot for CAD model generation and investigates the influence of prompt engineering on model quality. A benchmark dataset comprising 60 design tasks was developed and categorized into easy, intermediate, and complex levels. The benchmark included primitive geometries, polygonal and polyhedral models, mechanical components, hollow structures, assemblies, lattice designs, and advanced engineering systems. For each prompt, the generated STL file was evaluated based on geometric accuracy, completeness of requested features, and overall structural validity using commercial software. The results revealed a strong dependence of generation success on design complexity, with easy-level tasks exhibiting high first-attempt success rates, while intermediate and complex tasks frequently required prompt refinement. Prompt length alone was found to have minimal influence on performance; instead, successful CAD generation depended primarily on clearly specified dimensions, geometric features, and functional relationships. Overall, the findings demonstrate that generative AI can lower the barrier to CAD modeling for non-expert users while improving productivity for experienced designers, thereby offering significant potential for engineering design, rapid prototyping, and additive manufacturing applications.

items.title: Assessing the Learning Gains and User Experience of Large Language Model Simulations for Clinical Medical Education: A Pilot Observational Study
items.abstract: Background Medical students often struggle transitioning from preclinical coursework to clinical environments. Simulation-based training can bridge this gap but can be resource intensive. Large language models (LLMs) provide a scalable resource that can augment traditional training. However, their effects on learning outcomes and student perceptions are currently not understood. This study aims to evaluate medical student knowledge acquisition and perception of the utility of simplified LLM-based clinical simulation. Methods Using the RISE framework, a structured simulation was designed to assess medical student knowledge of acute asthma exacerbation management. ZotGPT, an institutional GPT-4 based platform was utilized. Medical students completed pre- and post-simulation assessments assessing knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of simulation utility. Subgroup analysis was stratified by time spent completing the simulation. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon signal-rank and McNemar tests. Results A total of 155 students participated. The simulation significantly improved perceived understanding of key treatment steps, including initial bronchodilator and steroid therapy (p = 0.001), magnesium sulfate escalation (p = 0.002), refractory management (p = 0.021), and discharge planning (p = 0.005). Students rated the simulation as more useful than non-simulation learning tools (p = 0.017) and noninferior to in-person simulation (p = 0.226). Confidence in asthma management increased (p < 0.001), but objective knowledge gains were not observed, with balanced correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct responses for intermediate steps. Longer engagement (> 600 seconds) was associated with greater perceived benefit. Simulations were deemed helpful for learning (94.7%), and most students preferred immediate feedback (68.4%). Conclusions LLM-based clinical simulations were well accepted, improved medical student confidence, and were perceived as educationally useful. However, objective knowledge gains were limited. LLMs thus may serve as an adjunctive educational tool but require improved prompt design, structured feedback, and guided implementation to optimize outcomes.

items.title: Associations between Anthropometric, Behavioral, and Psychosocial Factors and Low Back Pain among University Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: Low back pain (LBP) is a prevalent musculoskeletal condition among young adults and may negatively affect academic performance and quality of life. The contribution of anthropometric and lifestyle factors to LBP in university populations remains unclear. Objective: To examine the association between anthropometric parameters, behavioral factors, and LBP prevalence among university students. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 193 University students aged 18–27 years. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and standardized anthropometric measurements, including body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, hip circumference, and waist-to-hip ratio. LBP was self-reported. Associations were analyzed using chi-square tests, independent t-tests, and logistic regression. Effect sizes were expressed as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results: The prevalence of LBP was 75.1%. No significant associations were found between LBP and anthropometric variables, including BMI, waist circumference, and waist-to-hip ratio (p > 0.05). Behavioral factors such as physical activity, academic stress, and backpack use were also not significantly associated with LBP. Conclusion: LBP is highly prevalent among university students but was not associated with anthropometric or selected behavioral factors. Other determinants, including ergonomic and psychosocial factors, may play a more important role. Further longitudinal studies are recommended.Top of Form

items.title: Associations of managers’ AI literacy with innovative work behavior and work well-being through AI job crafting and psychological needs satisfaction
items.abstract: Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

items.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
items.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

items.title: Attenuated, Not Absent. Trusting Autonomous Systems Tracks Reliability More Closely, With Less Neural Engagement, Than Trusting Humans
items.abstract: Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system’s output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

items.title: Avatars of ourselves: Exploring professional identity with generative AI in business education
items.abstract: Convincing digital copies of professional selves, avatars that look, sound, and respond like a person, have become easier to produce with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). This paper reports work in progress on a postgraduate business subject at an Australian university, in which students explore professional identity by constructing, testing, and questioning AI representations of themselves. In a curriculum-embedded workshop, students choose between two equivalent activities: building an AI avatar from a self-authored knowledge base or writing a structured professional profile. Both ask students to decide deliberately what to share with, and withhold from, an AI system, then to test their representation against simulated professional scenarios before reflection and debrief. Drawing on postdigital perspectives, the design positions GenAI as neither threat nor solution but as a provocation for identity work. Both critical evaluation of technology and self-knowledge matter more when AI can convincingly represent a person. Preliminary findings from this first iteration, drawn from facilitator reflections and de-identified conversation logs, suggest that the pedagogical value of self-representing avatars lies in the critical questioning they provoke, rather than in their technical sophistication. The workshop offers a practical, adaptable model for critical and creative engagement with GenAI and professional identity.

items.title: Balancing Upward and Downward Communication in Multigenerational Workplaces: An Integrative Review and a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model
items.abstract: Organizations must combine clear downward direction with upward employee voice, and the age diversity of contemporary workforces is often presented as making this balance harder to achieve. This article examines that claim through an integrative review of research on organizational communication, employee voice and silence, psychological safety, organizational justice, and generational diversity. The review covers the four cohorts that dominate today's workforce (Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z), considers Generation Alpha prospectively, and sets boundaries for its central constructs: multigenerational workplace, downward and upward communication, communication balance, and communication equilibrium. Searches combined communication-direction, voice, and generation terms, supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of African journal platforms; sources were screened against explicit inclusion criteria, synthesized through data reduction, display, comparison, and verification, and each claim was graded as established, supported, or conjectural. Meta-analytic and consensus evidence shows that differences between generational cohorts in work attitudes are small and confounded with age and period effects. The article therefore proposes a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model (CEM), which starts from age diversity but locates its communicative effects in five proximal sources of variation: career stage, hierarchical role, digital access, work arrangement, and cultural orientation. The model specifies one downward condition (directive clarity), two upward conditions (psychological safety and leadership responsiveness), and one bidirectional condition (channel diversity), which together sustain directional balance, a state in which decision-makers act on clear direction and accurate upward information. Five assumptions underpin the model, and equilibrium is maintained by a balancing responsiveness loop that counters a reinforcing spiral of silence. Eight propositions, with indicators, levels of analysis, and evidential status, set out a research agenda that prioritizes designs separating age, period, and cohort effects and theory built from sub-Saharan African organizations, treating their employees as agents of voice rather than deviations from Northern norms.

items.title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
items.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.

items.title: Benchmarking Choice Consistency in Large Language Models: A Measurement-Theoretic Analysis of Transitivity Axiom
items.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as decision-makers, current evaluation practice emphasizes benchmark accuracy rather than the structural properties that make decisions coherent and interpretable. We introduce a measurement-theoretic framework for evaluating whether the choices of an LLM are transitively rationalizable, focusing on the choice axiom of transitivity of preference. When transitivity is violated over a choice set, alternatives can no longer be coherently ordered as globally better or worse, and a stated preference between one pair constrains nothing about how the model would choose between any others. We apply our framework across 20 distinct LLMs, systematically varying question format, generation temperature, and contextual memory, using classic choice paradigms previously shown to induce intransitive preferences in humans. We find substantial and systematic transitivity violations in many models, although some patterns partially mirror known features of human decision behavior. Testing the transitivity axiom thus offers a principled, complementary foundation for evaluating the consistency of AI decision making beyond benchmark accuracy.

items.title: Between risk and reform: Learning designers’ experiences of institutional responses to GenAI in assessment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
items.abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

items.title: Beyond association: Causal risk factors for e-scooter injury from a naturalistic riding study
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of shared e-scooter services has introduced a novel public health challenge, with rising injury rates reported globally. Existing epidemiological studies rely largely on retrospective hospital or police records, which lack data on pre-crash mechanisms. While naturalistic studies have begun to fill this gap, they have thus far relied on associational measures that may be biased by confounding. This study aims to quantify the causal effects of rider behavior and environmental factors on e-scooter safety–critical events (SCEs) using a formal causal inference framework. We conducted a case-control analysis within a naturalistic riding study of a public e-scooter service in Gothenburg, Sweden (2022–2023), drawing from 6868 trips. Our analysis included 61 SCEs (cases) and 183 randomly selected control events. We used directed acyclic graphs to identify confounders and applied the parametric g-formula weighted for exposure duration to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences. After adjustment, the risk of an SCE increased substantially for single-handed riding (RR = 5.5), riding through an intersection (RR = 3.8), and inexperience (RR = 2.8). Phone use was associated with an approximately threefold increase in risk (RR = 3.1), though this estimate was not statistically significant. Both rider behavior (e.g., inexperience, single-handed riding) and the built environment (e.g., intersections) are significant causal contributors to e-scooter crash risk. These findings provide evidence for a multi-level public health strategy that focuses on novice rider education, infrastructure modifications at intersections, and technological interventions to support riders during their trips.

items.title: Beyond checklists: A relational approach to UDL implementation
items.abstract: Although Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is grounded in principles of inclusion, flexibility, and learner variability, its implementation in higher education can become reduced to procedural or checklist-driven approaches, creating a tension between its human-centred philosophy and institutional practice. This paper adopts a reflective approach to examine the implementation of UDL across selected courses at an Australian university, exploring how shared understandings of inclusive teaching were co-constructed through dialogue between academics and an educational developer. The reflective inquiry suggests that meaningful UDL implementation is less dependent on frameworks than on relational, dialogic engagement through which pedagogical meaning is negotiated in context. At a time when higher education is increasingly shaped by digital technologies and artificial intelligence, the paper argues for re-centring relationships, collaboration, and human judgement as the foundation of meaningful curriculum transformation. In doing so, it positions educational developers as knowledge architects who facilitate the co-construction of inclusive pedagogical practice and offers a relational perspective on UDL implementation that may inform educational developers and academics seeking to implement inclusive curriculum renewal within their own institutional contexts.

items.title: Beyond conversation length: Conversation openings, cognitive engagement, and support orientations in student-AI chatbot interactions
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

items.title: Beyond corrective feedback: A learner-centred approach to GenAI feedback for EAL academic writing
items.abstract: Students in higher education are increasingly using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools in feedback for academic writing. This is important for English as an Additional Language (EAL) learners for whom immediate and accessible support in revising their writing, including its linguistic, rhetorical, and cultural dimensions, is particularly valuable. However, GenAI feedback cannot be assumed to be learner-centred simply because it is available and interactive, or that it appears to be fluent. This conceptual paper uses a learner-centred feedback framework, which foregrounds enabling sensemaking, focusing on future impact, and supporting agency, to examine GenAI feedback for EAL academic writing. It argues that GenAI feedback should be understood as a feedback process, the value of which depends on whether it enables EAL learners’ sensemaking, supports future writing development, and sustains learners’ agency in deciding how to use GenAI-generated feedback information. The paper contributes a learner-centred conceptualisation of GenAI feedback for EAL academic writers and offers practical considerations for designing feedback activities that support future impact, sensemaking, and agency.

items.title: Beyond graduate attributes: Embedding employability through reflective practice and work-integrated learning
items.abstract: Graduate employability has become a strategic priority across higher education, yet development of employability capabilities often remains fragmented, positioned outside the curriculum through co-curricular activities or graduate attribute frameworks that lack developmental coherence (Jackson & Bridgstock, 2021). This poster asks: how can employability capabilities be scaffolded longitudinally through reflective practice and Work-Integrated Learning to develop professional identity and career resilience in AI-enabled professional contexts? It presents the curriculum design rationale for the Bachelor of Applied Business at UNSW College, commencing October 2026, demonstrating how digital infrastructure, systematic reflection, and authentic workplace learning build career-ready graduates who work critically with emerging technologies. The design positions reflection not as an isolated assessment task but as career development pedagogy, building metacognitive capability, professional identity, and adaptive resilience across three years. This draws on foundational theories of reflective practice (Schön, 1992) and transformative learning (Mezirow, 1991), integrated with contemporary scholarship on professional identity formation (Jackson, 2016, 2017) and career adaptability (Savickas & Porfeli, 2012). The scaffolded architecture moves from foundational self-awareness tasks in Year 1, through applied workplace reflection during industry placements in Year 2, to integrative professional identity synthesis in the Year 3 capstone—providing authentic contexts for capability development throughout the degree. This progression is enabled through Canvas LMS integrated with the Stackle reflective learning platform. Stackle creates a longitudinal ePortfolio where students document reflective entries across all courses, receive structured prompts aligned to developmental focus, and build a cumulative narrative of professional growth. The curriculum embeds industry engagement through industry-informed assessment tasks across 100% of courses, formal placements, and a capstone industry project. Reflective practice is explicitly connected to each WIL experience through Stackle, requiring students to analyse workplace challenges and articulate capability development—an approach shown to strengthen pre-professional identity formation (Jackson, 2017; Trede et al., 2012). The platform enables integrated feedback from academic supervisors and industry mentors, making capability development visible to students, educators, and potential employers. Embedding AI fluency as a professional capability is central to this design. Rather than treating generative AI as peripheral or threatening to assessment integrity, the curriculum positions AI literacy as essential to contemporary professional practice. Students engage with transparent AI disclosure practices in reflection, use AI tools critically to analyse workplace data, and develop ethical reasoning frameworks for AI use. Assessment structures centre human judgment and applied problem-solving—reflective analysis, workplace challenge responses, and professional presentations—requiring critical thinking about AI outputs rather than uncritical acceptance. This responds to contemporary debates about authentic assessment in AI-mediated learning environments (Bearman et al., 2023), positioning graduates as professionals who work with AI critically and ethically. This poster presents: (1) the theoretical framework; (2) the three-year reflective practice progression model; (3) the WIL integration strategy with 100% industry-informed assessment; and (4) design principles for embedding AI fluency. The contribution is a replicable framework for embedding employability longitudinally while leveraging digital infrastructure to support human agency in AI-augmented professional contexts.

items.title: Beyond permission: Mapping generative AI policy approaches across Australian universities
items.abstract: Australian universities are revising generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) guidance under strong pressure to assure learning, academic integrity and assessment quality. This concise paper reports a public-source mapping of GenAI policy, assessment guidance and student AI-literacy preparation across the 38 Universities Australia member universities. Using six TEQSA sources as contextual material, 100 university sources were coded by authority level, dominant public guidance approach, assessment model and student-facing literacy support. The public evidence shows diverse policy configurations: 18 universities used a structured framework, scale, tier or lane model, while eight relied mainly on assessment-specific rules. Student preparation was also prominent: 19 universities provided formal AI-specific learning opportunities, and 12 provided structured student hubs or toolkits. The findings suggest that GenAI policy can function as curriculum infrastructure rather than only academic-integrity compliance. The paper contributes to Human-Centred Learning Design by treating GenAI policy as learning design infrastructure that connects assessment authority, student trust, feedback expectations and AI literacy.

items.title: Beyond Pixels: Visual Metaphor Transfer via Schema-Driven Agentic Reasoning
items.abstract: A visual metaphor constitutes a high-order form of human creativity, employing cross-domain semantic fusion to transform abstract concepts into impactful visual rhetoric. Despite the remarkable progress of generative AI, existing models remain largely confined to pixel-level instruction alignment and surface-level appearance preservation, failing to capture the underlying abstract logic necessary for genuine metaphorical generation. To bridge this gap, we introduce the task of Visual Metaphor Transfer (VMT), which challenges models to autonomously decouple the "creative essence" from a reference image and re-materialize that abstract logic onto a user-specified target subject. We propose a cognitive-inspired, multi-agent framework that operationalizes Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) through a novel Schema Grammar (\(\mathcal {SG}\)). This structured representation decouples relational invariants from specific visual entities, providing a rigorous foundation for cross-domain logic re-instantiation. Our pipeline executes VMT through a collaborative system of specialized agents: a perception agent that distills the reference into a schema, a transfer agent that maintains generic space invariance to discover apt carriers, a generation agent for high-fidelity synthesis and a hierarchical diagnostic agent that mimics a professional critic, performing closed-loop backtracking to identify and rectify errors across abstract logic, component selection, and prompt encoding. Extensive experiments and human evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in metaphor consistency, analogy appropriateness, and visual creativity, paving the way for automated high-impact creative applications in advertising and media. Project page with source code and self-contained skills is https://yuci-gpt.github.io/Beyond-Pixels/.

items.title: Beyond prompting: An epistemic agency framework for generative AI literacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally altered how learners access, construct, and engage with knowledge. Existing discussions of GenAI literacy have largely emphasised operational competencies, such as prompt engineering, understanding AI capabilities, and ethical use. While these competencies remain important, they do not fully address the epistemic challenges arising from AI-mediated knowledge production. This paper proposes reframing GenAI literacy through the lens of epistemic agency; that is, learners’ capacity to critically evaluate, regulate, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge generated in collaboration with intelligent systems. Rather than viewing GenAI literacy as a collection of technical skills, this conceptual paper argues that its primary educational purpose is to cultivate learners who can exercise informed judgement in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments. Building on existing AI literacy scholarship and theories of epistemic agency, the paper introduces a conceptual framework comprising four interrelated dimensions: epistemic evaluation, epistemic regulation, epistemic responsibility, and epistemic autonomy. The framework provides a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding how GenAI literacy can move beyond operational competence towards fostering independent, reflective, and responsible knowledge construction.

items.title: Beyond the Model: A Survey of Harness Software for Embodied Agents
items.abstract: Embodied foundation models produce impressive demonstrations, but executing long, complex tasks depends on software outside the model, just as in the ransition from ChatGPT to Codex. We call that software the embodied agent harness and divide it into planning, skill acquisition, memory, monitoring, and self-evolution. The papers come from robotics, machine learning, and embodied-AI venues, 2022--2026. About a fifth of the citations are preprints or non-archival manuscripts, mostly for new directions. Open problems remain in efficiency, robustness, generalizability, model availability, multi-robot orchestration, and evaluation.

items.title: Beyond the pretty graph: Human-centred assessment design for evaluative judgement
items.abstract: Assessment in data visualisation courses too often rewards technical output over communicating substance. When visualisation is taught as a tool rather than a discipline, students learn to produce work that meets the brief but has little to say. This paper reports on a course redesign that addresses this gap through a human-centred assessment design grounded in evaluative judgement theory, treating evaluative judgement as a capability exercised by both students and markers. The redesign is structured around five elements addressing student ownership of project topics, portfolio assessment, descriptive capability levels, practitioner modelling, and creative freedom within a structured framework, implemented in a required course within a Master of Data Science program. Practitioner inquiry into the operation of this design in the presence of generative AI revealed that AI functioned not as a threat to academic integrity but as a mechanism that raised creative ambition, shifting the limiting factor from technical skill to evaluative judgement. Although situated in a data visualisation course, the contribution is broader. As generative AI makes technical production easier, helping students develop the capacity to recognise, justify, and communicate insight becomes the central challenge across higher education, and this paper suggests one way to address it.
